title: The tables overturned (Matthew 21:12–13)
hookLine: the one time he makes a whip, and it's about the house of prayer

cards: The outer courts of the Temple in Jerusalem, a few days before Passover. Enormous, noisy, packed with pilgrims. They need animals for the sacrifices, so people are selling cattle and sheep and doves.
They need the right coins for the Temple, so money changers sit at their tables. The shouting, the bargaining, the animals, the clink of coins.
And Jesus walks in, the man who has spent weeks of our story healing, forgiving, eating with sinners, telling stories of lost sheep. And he starts turning over tables.

teach.h: COINS ON THE FLOOR, DOVES IN THE AIR.
teach.b: Matthew says Jesus cast out all who were buying and selling there, and overthrew the tables of the money changers, and the seats of those who sold doves. Coins rolling across the stone floor. Birds fluttering.
People shouting. Then he quotes scripture, in the Douay-Rheims: "My house shall be called the house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves."

He's joining two prophets: Isaiah, who promised that God's house would be a house of prayer, and Mark adds, for all nations; and Jeremiah, who warned against treating the Temple like a hideout for robbers.
So this isn't Jesus against the Temple. It's a Jewish teacher who loves the Temple, standing in the line of Israel's own prophets, demanding that it be what it's for.
The whip is in John's Gospel: he made a whip of cords and drove them all out, the sheep and the oxen too.

teach.h: A WHIP, TO CLEAR A SPACE.
teach.b: A whip, in the hands of the man who told the story of the lost sheep, and he uses it to clear a space for prayer. And watch what happens next in Matthew.

teach.h: THEN THE BLIND AND THE LAME COME IN.
teach.b: The blind and the lame come to him in the Temple, and he heals them. The space gets cleared, and then filled, with the people who needed it most.
Catholics hear another layer too: Saint Paul writes that you yourselves are God's temple, and that his Spirit lives in you.

teach.h: MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.
teach.b: The Church reads John's version of this story in Lent, a season for clearing out the clutter so there's room for prayer.

how: Catholics hear John's account of the cleansing of the Temple on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year B, and many treat the season as a time to clear out habits and clutter to make room for prayer.

o: a sharp rebuke spoken to scold the money changers
a lash made of cords, used to drive the animals out
a staff carried by shepherds to guide their sheep

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus is against the Temple itself
he quotes Israel's prophets and demands the Temple be what it's for: a house of prayer.
after he clears the courts, the blind and the lame come and he heals them
the space is cleared, then filled with the people who needed it.
all four Gospels mention the whip
only John mentions the whip of cords.

games.q: you're Jesus, walking into the Temple courts at the festival. they're full of trading and noise. what do you do?
o: walk past and find a quiet corner.
overturn the tables and quote the prophets.
games.why: he overturns the tables: “My house shall be called the house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves.”

practice: Think of a space in your life meant for one thing that has filled up with everything else: a desk, a corner of your room, the first ten minutes of your morning eaten by the phone, your own head.
Picture the tables going over, gently, the clutter cleared and the space open again, and ask what you'd want that space to be for. If you pray, you can ask for a house of prayer inside you.

wordCard.voice: whip. What John's Gospel says Jesus made of cords, to drive the money changers from the Temple courts.

orig.note: Greek: house of prayer, the Gospel's words for Isaiah's phrase that Jesus quotes.

carryVoice: Your line: a house of prayer. Cleared, and then filled. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: My house shall be called the house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves.
